passage: Anand, you've been sending everything home, haven't you? I can see it in your lunch box. Let me tell you. At twenty-four I was a clerk in Kolkata, and every rupee went to my village: my brothers' schooling, my father's debts, my sister's wedding. I loved them. I also, secretly, hated opening my wallet. Then I hated myself for hating it. One Eid I went home and my brother asked for a motorcycle. Something in me snapped, and I shouted. My mother sat me down afterwards. That night I, Tanvir, finally said it plainly: "I'll pay for schooling. Not motorcycles. I need to build my own home too." They were hurt for a month. Then they understood. passage:
January: Trisha made a chart: swim twenty lengths without stopping by March, top three in the district by June. Every evening she logged her times. When her brother Vijay asked her to watch a film, she said, "No time."
April: She hit twenty lengths two weeks early. That night she felt restless rather than happy, and wrote a new target before bed. She'd stopped going to her friend's Saturday lunches.
June, after the district meet: She came fourth. She sat in the car, silent, feeling worthless. Vijay handed her a samosa. "You swam your best time ever. Also, you've been missing. We miss you." She looked out at the rain, then leaned against his shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Trisha finish at the district meet?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after coming fourth?
qa.a: She felt worthless, as if the result was the only measure of her.

qa.q: How did Vijay help Trisha?
qa.a: He pointed out her best time and told her the family missed her, reminding her she is more than a result.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay when Trisha keeps saying "No time"?
qa.a: Vijay probably feels shut out and misses his sister.

grounding: Shows over months a goal-driven teen whose worth becomes tied to results as rest and relationships slip.

passage: You set targets like I did, beta. At fifteen I had a notebook of goals: first in class, state chess, a hundred push-ups. I ticked them all. And each time I felt a flat hunger instead of joy, and wrote a bigger one. My friend Sharmila used to come by with raw mangoes and salt, and I'd send her away: "Studying." One day she stopped coming. In the board exam I came first in the district. My photo was in the newspaper. I, Eshaan, sat alone in my room with that newspaper and felt nothing. That was my turning point. I walked to Sharmila's house with salt and two mangoes. She laughed at me for an hour. I still set goals. I also keep Sundays for mangoes.

qa.q: What did Sharmila bring when she visited?
qa.a: Raw mangoes and salt.

qa.q: What did young Eshaan feel sitting with the newspaper?
qa.a: Eshaan felt empty, with nothing, despite coming first in the district.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Feeling nothing after the success made Eshaan walk to Sharmila's house with mangoes, choosing friendship again.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when she was sent away again and again?
qa.a: Sharmila likely felt hurt and unwanted, so she stopped coming.

grounding: Shows a goal-driven teen for whom success became the only measure until its emptiness led back to a friendship.

passage: People keep asking me for my five-year plan. I'm Kashish, twenty-one, and honestly, my plan is to get really, truly good at tabla. Not famous. Good. I practise four hours every morning before college, the same bol over and over till my wrists ache, and I record myself so I can hear what's still muddy. My friend Indu thinks I'm wasting myself: "You could do an MBA, you're smart." She means well. My cousins think I'm lazy because I don't post my practice online or enter every competition. But last month my guru nodded once, just once, at my tirakita. That's the whole thing for me. That nod. I'm not in a hurry.

qa.q: How many hours does Kashish practise each morning?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when the guru nodded?
qa.a: Kashish felt deeply satisfied and proud, since that nod mattered more than any title.

qa.q: What would you advise Kashish's cousins before calling Kashish lazy?

qa.q: How does Indu see Kashish's path?
qa.a: Indu thinks Kashish is wasting talent and should do an MBA, though she means well.

grounding: Shows a young adult quietly devoted to mastering a craft rather than status, misread by others as lacking drive.

passage:

December: The bowls were getting thinner, the walls more even. Sharmila's parents, visiting, asked Arohi what she wanted to become. She said, "Good at pots." They exchanged a look.
March: The ceramics professor picked one of her bowls to show the first-years as an example of a true centre. Arohi said nothing to anyone. Back in the room, she wrote the date in her notebook and smiled.

passage: Aparna, you asked why I never took the manager's job at the mill. At twenty I was a weaver's apprentice in Chanderi, and all I wanted was to make a border so fine you couldn't see where one thread ended. My cousins got clerk jobs and laughed at me: "Still at the loom? No ambition." My mother worried too. But every day I sat with old Master Rehmat and redid the same paisley until my eyes watered. I, Usha, didn't tell anyone my goals. They were mine. Years later a buyer from Delhi picked up one of my saris and held it to the light without a word. That silence was the prize I had been working for.

qa.q: Who did young Usha sit with every day?
qa.a: Old Master Rehmat.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel about those goals?
qa.a: Usha felt determined and quietly private, caring about fine work more than status.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The Delhi buyer silently holding the sari to the light showed that years of practice had reached true mastery.

qa.q: How did Usha's cousins see that choice?
qa.a: They laughed and thought Usha had no ambition because Usha stayed at the loom.

grounding: Shows a young adult's quiet, private ambition to master a craft, misread by others as lack of drive.

passage: When the state engineering entrance results came out, Himani's rank was in the top hundred, and by evening the whole of Kotdwar knew. Her father handed out sweets; her uncle posted her photo in the family group; strangers stopped her outside the chemist's. She smiled for everyone. That night she sat on the roof with her friend Gargi and felt strangely empty, as if she'd climbed a staircase to an empty room. "I did it for Papa's face at the sweet shop," she said slowly. "I don't even know if I like engineering." Gargi didn't answer right away. Then: "What would you want, if nobody was watching?" Himani looked at the dark hills for a long time. She didn't have an answer yet.

qa.q: Where did Himani's uncle post her photo?
qa.a: In the family group.

qa.q: How did Himani feel on the roof that night?
qa.a: She felt strangely empty, as if she'd climbed a staircase to an empty room.

qa.q: What question could help Himani redirect her ambition?
qa.a: Gargi's question about what she would want if nobody was watching.

qa.q: How does Himani's father experience the result?
qa.a: He is proud and delighted, handing out sweets to everyone.

grounding: Shows a student who chased a rank to impress family and feels hollow after reaching it, prompted to ask whose approval she seeks.

passage: Beatriz had printed the logo of the city's most famous law firm and taped it above her desk in the São Paulo dorm. For two years she chased it: top grades, the right societies, the right parties. When the internship offer came, she posted a photo within minutes. Four hundred likes. Her mother called, crying with pride. Then Beatriz sat in her room and felt nothing much at all. Her roommate Mei, who was taking a lower-paid job at a legal-aid clinic because she loved the work, came in humming. Beatriz watched her, and a question she had avoided for two years arrived: whose dream is this? She took down the logo and looked at the pale rectangle it left on the wall.

qa.q: How many likes did Beatriz's photo get?
qa.a: Four hundred likes.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel after getting the internship?
qa.a: She felt hollow, nothing much at all, despite the likes and her mother's pride.

qa.q: What step might help Beatriz redirect her ambition?
qa.a: Reflecting on whose dream she has been chasing and what work she would love, as Mei does.

qa.q: How does Mei seem to feel about her lower-paid job?
qa.a: Mei seems happy and content, humming because she loves the work.

grounding: Illustrates a student chasing a prestigious name for approval, feeling hollow on arrival and beginning to question whose dream it is.

passage: In the convocation hall of the engineering college in Coimbatore, Keerthana walked up for the gold medal while her parents filmed from the third row. She had planned this moment since first year: every late night, every skipped trip, for this. Afterwards, in the corridor, she felt oddly flat, the medal heavy against her chest. Uma-ma'am, her project guide, found her by the water cooler. "You don't look happy." "I thought I'd feel something," Keerthana admitted. "It was for Appa, I think. And for the girls who said I'd never make it." Uma-ma'am nodded. "And the chip-design work you did at two in the morning because you loved it? Who was that for?" Keerthana was quiet. Then, slowly, she smiled.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana's parents film from?
qa.a: The third row.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after receiving the medal?
qa.a: She felt oddly flat and hollow, the medal heavy against her chest.

qa.q: How did Uma-ma'am help Keerthana?
qa.a: By asking who the chip-design work was for, pointing her to what she truly loved.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's parents feel filming the ceremony?
qa.a: They are likely proud and happy, unaware of how flat she feels.

grounding: Shows a student who chased a medal for others' approval, feels hollow, and is guided to reflect on what she really values.
